Department of .Labour-Industrial Investigation Act, $25,000.
Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour) Before taking up this item I desire to make a very brief statement concerning the expenditures of the Department of Labour, chiefly for the purpose of correcting two or three mis-statements that have been made respecting them. Some time ago the lion, member for Rouville, in criticising the expenditures of the various departments, stated that there had been an increase in the total expenditure of the Department of Labour between the years 1911 and 1915 of 50 per cent. On being challenged, he declared that he would prove his statement up to the hilt when we came to the estimates.
Did I make that statement this session or last?

Last session. The Public Accounts show that for the first full year
>
after we were in power, namely, from March 31, 1912 to March 31, 1913, the expenditure of the Department of Labour, instead of being 50 per cent more than the expenditure in the last full year of our predecessors, namely 1910-1911, was 17 per cent less, and last year, 1915-16, our expenditure was 15 per cent less than in the last full year of our predecessors. Our expenditure last year, ending on March 31, the figures for which do not appear in the Auditor-General's report, but which I have made up, was about $700 less than the year before, and 15 per cent less than the last year hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. So that instead of the expenditures of the Department of Labour having increased by 50 per cent, there was a decrease of 17 per cent the first year we were in power, and of 15 per cent in the last two years. My hon. friend from Assiniboia, discussing the same subject, though I think he must have got his information from a different source, said that the expenditures of the Department of Labour for the last four years showed an increase over the expenditure when the hon. gentlemen opposite were in power of 32 per cent. The explanation I have just given in answer to the statement of my hon. friend from Rouville covers also the statement of my hon. friend from Assiniboia. If I may repeat, the decrease the first year we were in power was 17 per cent, and last year and the year before there was a decrease of about 15 per cent instead of an increase of 50 per cent or 32 per cent.
Labour - Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, $25,000.

Might I suggest that
this sum is not nearly large enough, if it includes anything more than simple investigation or incipient preliminary inquiry. Surely, the House ought to have grasped the fact that labour is something of a more extended character than simply the pulling back and forward of interests called' labour. It has too long been the fashion 'to suppose that the time would come when we should arrive at some settled point. That settled point never can be arrived at in labour, I submit, any more than in any other branch of economics. It is precisely like phenomena of meteorology. You never cam tell where an eddy of air is, going to work out at any one time. The economic equilibrium can never be attained. I would not say that it is a mathematical impossibility, but it is certainly a human impossibility; and, since there

are different people in tlie world, different dispositions, rivalries, various elements, that go to make up all these different currents, it must follow that there can never be a precise equilibrium. The effect will always manifest itself in continual upheaval. For people to say that we have arrived at the milennium because the minimum wage of labour is so and so, is to state what may be true at this moment; but, having- regard to the theory of rent, having regard to the Malthusian doctrine, having regard to the theories of John Stuart Mill, or any other elementary writer on political economy-Thorold Rogers, or anybody else you like-it will be seen at a glance that i't is simply one horse pulling against another in the great economic struggle, and you never can tell which is going to be ahead; one appears to be ahead and satisfied, but in a moment it is pulled back and the other is ahead; and so this struggle goes on. To maintain the fair, impartial and true condition of the whole economic world is the duty of the legislators of the nation; that iis the duty of the members of this House, and particularly of our expert, the Minister of Labour. That being the case, why cut down to -a paltry sum the investigation into one of the very few great elements of the whole economic struggle? I am sure the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) will rise in his place -and reassert such a simple principle as that. We are so continually doing things in what we call the law, >an -adi captandum way-continually plastering up one little hole, or dealing with one little difficulty, never realizing that there is an underlying principle which, if we once ascertain it, gives us the solution of the problem. We must get out of this fashion, or else cease to call ourselves cultivated and scientific. It is just as in the study of zoology, or comparative anatomy, it is a question of life, of living beings', and what is needed is an analysis of experience in order to enable us to understand the elements of the problem we have to face. We shall not reach the solution by considering separately such questions as the price of flour, or the rate of wages. That is absurd. It does not matter what these are, so long as they are in equipose.
Would the hon. gentleman say how much additional would establish the equilibrium he has advocated?

I would reply by saying that I am criticising the disposition
to pare down this item. That is all.
Mr. LUC'IEN PACAUD (Megantic): I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to bring before this committee the facts disclosed to us by the documents brought down by the Minister of Labour in connection with the strike at Thetford Mines. In doing so, it is not my intention to elaborate at any great length the views I hold, nor is it my intention to indulge in any extensive criticisms which, though they may be, I am sure, quite proper, quite just, quite well-founded, would most likely fall on deaf ears so far as concerns the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers). My one object in rising is this:	The miners of Thetford
Mines have a just grievance against the Minister of Labour for the most extraordinary attitude which he saw fit to take at the time of our strike last year. As I share that grievance and as I am their representative, I intend to voice our grievance before this committee, and to set forth the facts which gave rise to them. At the beginning of June, 1916, a situation arising out of difficulties between the asbestos companies and the miners became most acute. There seemed at that time no ground for a compromise between the men and the companies. The Department of Labour was officially notified of this situation by a letter which I hold in my hand, written by the Secretary of tbo Western Federation of Miners on the 20th pf June, 1916:
To the Director of Inquiries,
Department of Labour, Ottawa.
Sir,-Would you be kind enough to send me immediately a copy of the Industrial Disputes Act, with all its amendments, the by-laws passed in conformity with this law, and also the blank forms necessary to make a formal request for a board? Does Article 57 of this law require that a notice of thirty days be given by the employees to the employers who desire a raise of salary of fifty cents per day, before making their request for ah inquiry?
Believe me,
Yours very truly,
L. J. L. Rousseau.
I received the first surprise of many which the perusal of the documents gave me when I ascertained that this letter was not included among these documents. I waive my right, for the present, to make any comment on this point. But I may add that there was no answe.r to this letter. So, on June 27-seven days later-Mr. Rousseau wrote a second letter as follows:
To the Director of Inquiries,
Department of Labour,
Ottawa.
Sir,-We have here a thousand of our members who are not satisfied with the condition of labour, and who have decided to strike if they

do not get satisfaction. A request for a raise of salary has been made and the employers have decided of refusing our request. We are actually taking a vote, which will close on the 1st July, and we have reason to believe that the vast majority is in favour of a strike. We, the officers of the Federation, are endeavouring to obtain a compromise between employees and employers. The, 20th instant I asked for blank forms necessary to make our request for inquiry, and you did not answer our letter. Please let me know if you still have these forms or better still, to send me them. If there are no special forms I would be very much obliged if you will inform me upon this matter.
L. J. L, Rousseau,
For the Union of Asbestos Miners W.F.U.
I may say that this letter was also not amongst the documents laid on the table of the House.
What is the date of that?

The 27th of June. The department replied on the 29th June, 1916. I may say immediately that I consider this letter the most important of all those written, or received, by the department in connection with this case. It was not on the file with the documents brought down. Here is the letter:
Deputy Minister of Labour, Canada.
Ottawa, 29th June, 1916.
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter.of the 27th of June, and in answer I am enclosing you four copies of the forms prepared by this office for a request for a council of conciliation and enquiry. We had not noticed that your letter of the 28th of June contained such a request. I hope that the officers of the Federation will continue to do their best to settle amicably these differences, and if this cannot be done through direct negotiations, that the employees will request a council of conciliation and enquiry. There are no special by-laws on this point, but you will find in the forms which we are addressing you, the printed information touching certain details, and in following closely these institutions, the petitioners would evade all errors.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd.) F. A. Acland, Deputy Minister of Labour.
Mr. L. J. L. Rousseau,
Thetford Mines, Que.
I will call the special attention of the minister to this part of the letter. This was a true declaration of policy on the part of the department. The minister was giving in this letter his intention, or the intention of his department, to follow the strict letter of the law as it is laid down in the Industrial Disputes Act 1907:
I hope that the officers of the Federation will continue to do their best to settle amicably

their differences, and if this cannot be done through direct negotiations, that the employees will request a council of conciliation and enquiry.
I will refer to this a little later on.
Who signs that?

F. A. Acland, Deputy
Minister of Labour. I have a, letter dated the 30th June and addressed to Mr. Rousseau which is of secondary importance. It informs Mr. Rousseau that:
Mr. Narcisse Arcand, one of the officers of this department, has been charged to go to Thetford Mines and to give you all the assistance to settle amicably the differences arising between the employers and the employees.
Before I go any further I hope the minister will he in a position to tell us exactly what was the work that was performed by Mr. Arcand at Thetford. He was sent there by the department, but I notice in the documents brought down by the minister there is no mention of him at all. I know he was aronnd there for a week or so, and I understand he was dismissed from the service. I do not know if it was in connection with that strike or not. Negotiations ^fent on between the 30th June, the time of the arrival of Mr. Arcand, and the 15t'h July. Then a petition was sent to the department. This petition requested a board of conciliation. I notice that in this petition there are three special points. First, it was declared that the cause of the dispute was that the present wages were not in proportion to the high cost of living. The petition is in French, and it says:-
The cause and the nature of the difference is that the present wages are not in proportion to the high cost of living.
In the second place, they note that 90 per cent of the men had voted in favour of a strike, but that the officers had decided to ask for a report. In the third place, it was stated that direct negotiations were impossible in view of the fact that the employers had stated that no concessions would he made. I wish to direct attention to this point in the petition that Mr. Sharpe, manager of the Asbestos Corporation of Canada, had declared to the men that he had absolutely no concessions to make. Therefore, to return to the letter of the 29th June from the department, i't was stated that if negotiations failed the men would only 'have to apply for a board and it would be granted. That letter was in reply to the letter of the 27th, which made reference to the possibility of a strike, and, therefore, the letter of the 29th could only have that one meaning. Therefore, on the 15th July, when the

petition was sent to the department, the minister knew that direct negotiations were at an end, because, in order to have direct negotiations, there must be two parties. One of the parties having said that he was not going to make any concessions whatever, the men had an absolute reply to the letter of the 29th of June, and they sent forward their petition. That was on the 15th July. On the 24th July the department sent the following letter to Mr. Rousseau:-
Department of Labour,
Canada.
Ottawa, 24th July, 1916.
Re-law of enquiries in matters of industrial disputes of 1907, concerning the differences between the proprietor of the Asbestos Mines at Thetford Mines, Quebec, and their employees, members of the local Union, No. 143 of the Western Federation of Miners.
Sir,
I have the honour to acknowledge reception of a petition signed by Mr. Joseph VallCe, and by yourself, as President and Secretary of the local Union 143 of the Western Federation of Miners, requesting the establishment by the miners of a commission of conciliation and enquiry by virtue of the law of enquiries in matters of industrial disputes, 1907. The petition does not mention clearly that yourself and Mr. Vallfie had informed the employees of the information given out at the time of your conference in the office of the Minister about one or two weeks ago, with the representatives of the principal Asbestos companies.
The questions which the petition claims are in dispute comprise the recognition of the Union, the check of system, etc. The opinion of the Minister is that these questions cannot be properly submitted to a commission of conciliation to be settled, and that it seems understood that the question of the recognition was not to be regarded as vital and was given up. As for the claim for a raise of wages, the conversation held in the office of the Minister established, you will remember, that a raise of salary having been given during the month of April last, and that the representatives of the company and of the employees at that meeting seemed to have come then at the conclusion that no advantage would probably result from a new agitation of this question at the present time.
The opinion of the Minister is, in the first place, that the employees of each company should be informed by Mr. VallSe or by yourself of the general nature and of the results of this discussion in question ; and, in the second place, that the pending questions should be discussed with each company separately, through the medium of a committee of employees, and you will remember that the Minister obtained for the Secretary of the Union the privilege of accompanying the committee of employees and to plead their cause. In proceeding along these principles, the employees will act in accordance with the entente which have been arrived at in the office of the Minister.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) F. A. ACLAND, Deputy-Minister of Labour, and Clerk of the Commission of Conciliation and Enquiry. Mr. L. J. L. Rousseau,
Thetford Mines, Que.
I think that before going -any further it would be well to summarize the position taken by the minister. On the 27th of June, he received a letter from the men informing him that the situation at Thetford is serious, that on the 1st of July they intended to take a vote as to whether or not they would go on strike. On the 29th, the minister writes acknowledging the receipt of this letter and telling the men: We aTe pleased that you are trying to negotiate; continue your negotiations and if you are not successful ask for a Board of Conciliation. In the petition of the 15th of July it was cleariy established and proved that direct negotiations were impossible, and the petitioners requested, not a favour, but the application of the law. The minister acknowledges the receipt of the petition on the 24th of July and then he says: But there is no more ground for a Board of conciliation; you, Mr. Vallee or Mr. Rousseau, go and see individually every miner, 2,000 of them; and after you have seen them individually and told them what happened in my office in April, that is six months before, go and see every employer and tell him what happened in our office at that time.' All of this was in the letter of the 24th of July, although we do not find it in the letter of the 29th of June. This letter was answered by Mr. Rousseau in the name of the union:
Thetford Mines, 28th July, 1916. The Clerk of the Commission of Conciliation and Enquiry,
Sir:-
In answer to your letter dated the 24th of July I wish to tell you that we do not see why our petition requesting a commission of 'conciliation and enquiry should contain clearly that we had previously informed our members of the information gathered at our conference at Ottawa, so that it would be accepted. As a matter of fact, we had informed our members of all the details of our interview with you. We take the permission of calling your attention on the fact that the points in dispute are: raising of salary from $2.00 to $2.50, that is to say approximately 25 per cent on the salaries as they are to-day.
During April last, it is true that there was a raise of 25 cents as an average, but taking into consideration the rising cost of living which is constant, our members have decided to claim this new raise of wages of 50 cents per day which is most reasonable and below the salaries paid in other parts of Canada.
We must consider further that our members do not work when the weather is bad, which is not the exception in our locality. You tell us in. your letter that the opinion of the Minister is that the miners of each company should submit and discuss with each manager separately the questions in dispute. We differ totally with you. His opinion would perhaps be good, if we were not organized as a labour union, but as such is the case, the moment that

our union by a vote taken at a meeting especially called to discuss such a demand, that decision becomes collective and applies to all the companies indiscriminately where our members are employed. If the opinion of the Minister was followed in the present case, we would have to follow it in cases where a trade union is engaged in about 500 different industries, which would be an impossibility and proves that that opinion is not conformable neither to the spirit nor to the letter of the law on industrial disputes. Nevertheless, we have fulfilled his desire through protesting on the interpretation given by the minister, and here is the result of our interviews. Mr. Hammerick, of the Jacob Asbestos, refused to grant the wish of the Minister in allowing me to accompany the delegation of miners from his mines. His answer was that his company could probably pay the salary that was requested but he did not know what to do under the circumstances. Mr. Johnson was amiable enough to meet the desire of the miners and he said in substance: that the raise of wages was favorable and agreeable to him, but that it would be necessary to come to an understanding with the other miners. Hon. J. It. Smith refused to recognize the advice of the Minister. We tried to meet Messrs Sharp & Bennett, but we were unable to do so due to their numerous occupations, v A great many people are enticing our men to strike. The detectives are daily repeating to our men: Hold on, you will win out. We cannot keep our men any longer. We have had to-night a general meeting and it was unanimously resolved that the workmen considered that they should not wait any longer for a Board of Arbitration. If in the 2nd of August it is not granted, we will take a decision. We therefore renew our request for a Board of Arbitration and attract the attention on the fact that it is impossible for us to prevent our members any longer to go on strike if this Board is not nominated in the very near future, and we disclaim any responsibility for the situation which might arise as we have given evidence of patiotism in preventing up to this date a strike at the mine at Thetford Mines and that we have conformed ourselves to the laws which govern this country in making application for a Board of Arbitration.
Yours very truly,
(Signed) L. J. L. Rousseau,
Secretary, W.F.M.
Then we have Mr. Rousseau on the 29th of July again sending a telegram to the clerk of the council of conciliation and inquiry:
Thetford Mines, 29th July, 1916.
To the Clerk of the Council of Conciliation and Enquiry, Department of Labor, Ottawa, Ont.,-
Our interview with the miners of the mines has not had the success which was expected. At a meeting held the same night, we have passed a resolution to inform you that if a Board of Arbitration is not granted on the 2nd of August, we shall no longer wait. I am writing you the details.
(Signed) L. J. L. Rousseau.
The only reply that the men got to that latter was this, on the 31st July, 1916, from the Assistant Deputy Minister of Labour:

Ottawa, 31st July, 1916. Deputy Minister of Labour,
Canada.
Sir,-I have the honor to acknowledge reception of your telegram concerning the actual differences between the employers and several of their employees at the asbestos mines of the district of Thetford Mines. We are taking measures which we hope will obviate the necessity of establishing a commission of conciliation and enquiry.
Anything but a Board of Conciliation.
In any case this department will not fail to make the greatest efforts in its power in the interest of peace and to assure the rights of the respective parties. We are. waiting for the reception of the details promised in your telegram.
Yours very truly,
(Signed) Gerald H. Brown, Assistant Deputy Minister of Labor. Mr. L. J. L. Rousseau,
Thetford Mines.
Now we come to the culmination. The men had waited in vain. They informed the department officially on the 20th of June of their intention to take action, but the 3rd of August, 1916, arrived and nothing had been done. Then the minister received this telegram:
A general strike has been declared this morning at 7.30. The men are nearly all out of work.
L. J. L. Rousseau.
And I see on the 3rd of August a telegram to J. L. Rousseau:
Mr. Blanchet will be in Thetford Mines tomorrow to make public investigation. Have men continue work meantime.
(Sgd.) T. W. Crothers.
But the strike had already been declared. Mr. Blanchet came to Thetford. There was a very large meeting at St. Maurice, one of the sections of the town. The people had been informed that the department would send a man, but it was a great disappointment to them as everybody spoke but Mr. Blanchet, so that we did not know what mission he had. After the strike had been on for one week, on the 10th of August, 1916, the men had a letter from the minister as follows:
Ottawa, 10th of August, 1917. Dear Mr. Rousseau,-
I was very much grieved to learn that the miners of Thetford Mines had left their work a few days ago, a fact which I cannot help but think was not at all wise, especially at a time when negotiations were going on in view of a settlement by agreement.
And this is after all the correspondence I have placed on Hansard to-night.
"When the war broke out, I addressed to the employers and to the employees a special de-

mancl to evade everywhere where it would be possible all labour difficulties, and I am happy to know that that line of conduct was generally followed by the two parties.
It is of the greatest importance for the workmeh that all their efforts which tend to better their condition should be such as to attract the sympathy of the public in general, for if they have not the public opinion behind them, these efforts would not be crowned with any permanent success, and especially during the war, public opinion is decidedly opposed to any cessation of work. The product of the mines at Thetford is of urgent necessity for the pursuance of the war and it is, I believe, the duty of the employees to return immediately to their work, and if it is necessary they could continue negotiations in view of bettering their condition.
I hope that you will be able to use your influence to bring about a just and reasonable settlement of the present difficulty and at all events to persuade the employees to return to work. I understand that the operators are ready to raise the wages by 25 cents per day, and I believe that if this is true it would be to the better interest of the employees to accept this offer. I fervently desire that the employees should everywhere receive fair treatment, but at the same time I am strongly of the opinion that under the circumstances the workmen of the mines at Thetford should accept this offer and return immediately to work.
With kindest regards, I remain,
Tours truly
Mr. J. 1,. J. Rousseau,
Thetford Mines, P.Q.
The letter was not signed, but I presume it was from the minister. It is addressed to Mr. L. J. L. Rousseau, Thetford Mines, Quebec.
The most important fact brought out by this letter is that the minister did not consider that the strike was a serious matter. He recognizes the importance of the operation of the mines, in view of the war, but he does nothing to prevent the strike. He goes back on what he said in his previous letter. He is notified on July 30 by telegram and letter that on August 2 there would be a strike unless the law were applied. Although he recognizes it as urgent in view of the war that the strike should be prevented, this is the course he took: he passed an Order in Council dated August 3, sending Mr. Blanchet to Thetford to prevent the strike-after the strike had been declared.
But the miners of Thetford Mines were not to be denied consideration. They took to heart the little reproach of the minister and they sent him the following reply:
To the Honourable T. W. Crothers,
Minister of Labour,
Parliament Buildings, Ottawa. Mr. the Minister;
We have at hand your letter of the 10th
instant. In reply I wish to inform you that
we have already acted in line with your wishes and that from the 10th of August last, the date on which you wrote us, the labour union of which I am the secretary had already given its assent to a resolution passed by a group of citizens of Thetford Mines, accepted at a meeting in which merchants and business men who are not workmen at the mines, but who have at heart the immediate settlement of these differences. You will see in reading a copy of this resolution, which accompanies my letter, that there is nothing excessively hard nor severe for the employers. It does not seem though that the latter have manifested any desire to accept it. The men belonging to the local catholic union have not as yet replied to the committee of citizens that they were ready to accept. We will add that as you informed us that the product of our men is of urgent necessity for the pursuance of the war, and that it was a patriotic duty for us to make certain sacrifices so as not to diminish this production. The union of which I am the secretary is right to accept an agreement still less severe for the employers and which ia as follows:
1.	The salary of all the workmen will be of $0.25 per day higher than it was at the month of July last.
2.	This scale of wages would remain in force during one year.
I have here a letter from Mr. Deschamps, attorney-at-law of Thetford Mines, who was secretary of the meeting of citizens at Thetford Mines which had been convened by the mayor. The letter is as follows:
Thetford Mines,
August 10th, 1916.
Mr. Joseph Vallfie,
President International Miners, P.Q.
Dear Sir,
At a meeting at Thetford Mines specially convened by His Honour the Mayor and held at the City Hall this day at 3.30 p.m., it was resolved unanimously to submit to the proprietors of the mines and also to the Labour Union a project of settlement which was submitted by His Honour the Mayor, of which a copy is herewith enclosed.
You will oblige me by giving me as soon as possible a reply informing me if your union accepts this project, so that I may be able to submit your reply at the next meeting.
I do not feel .that it is necessary to read this agreement. It is in absolute conformity with the terms of the letter written by the minister on August 10. The men had agreed to receive 25 cents a day.
I have given all the facts in this matter. The minister had one of two courses to follow: to respect the law or to evade it. He preferred to follow the latter course and to refuse a board of arbitration requested by the men, the law being very clear on this point. As a result of this refusal on his part for reasons which I do not wish to unveil, this body of men received more unfair treatment-I myself was a witness of what happened-than was ever accorded

to anybody in this country at the hands of a minister of the Crown.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Thetford Mines
is in the county that my hon. friend has the honour of representing in this House. He lives and practices law in Thetford Mines, and I am very much surprised that a lawyer should make such a deliverance as he has just made to the committee. He says that he has told us all the facts; I do not think he has. There were six separate corporations mining asbestos at Thetford Mines. There were two labour organizations there, a local one called the Catholic Association and the other the Western Federation of Miners. My hon. friend does not, perhaps, know all the facts, because three or four parties from Thetford Mines came to Ottawa on two .occasions, first of their own accord, and the second time at my request. If the hon. gentleman had read the Industrial Disputes Investion Act he would not have made the speech that he has just made. Five minutes examination of that Act would have shown him that it does not lend itself tp the establishment of a 'board of conciliation in the circumstances that existed at Thetford Mines. The first letter that he read from my deputy or myself was written at a time when we did not know anything about there being five other corporations or about the members of these labour organizations working at the six different mines. I am speaking from recollection because I have not any of the papers here. I am surprised that my hon. friend -should have brought the matter up at all, it is so perfectly plain that the case was not one in which a board of conciliation could have been properly established. Two thousand five hundred men belonging to these two different organizations were working in the six mines, if I remember rightly, about 1,200 belonging to each organization. I have on many occasions pointed out that where similar circumstances existed, the Act did not permit the establishment of a board of conciliation.
Why not?

I am coming to that now. One very prominent case occurred at Cobalt, where the miners were members of the same organization, the Western Federation of Miners. There were forty separate and distinct mines, with forty separate and distinct corporations running them, and we were asked to appoint a board of conciliation to investigate

the conditions in those forty different mines, each one of which would have been entitled to name one of the members of that board. When I pointed out the facts and stated that the Act did not lefid itself to any such action and suggested that we appoint a commission to inquire into the conditions in the forty mines, our suggestion was accepted; a commission was appointed, the investigation was made, and we have had no trouble since. Another case occurred at Toronto and Hamilton, where about a year ago a large number of machinists working in about half a hundred different factories asked for a board of conciliation. Each one of the fifty odd employers would have been entitled under the Act to name a member of that board, so, of course, I pointed out at once that we could not do anything of that kind, and I appointed another commission of three men, who investigated matters in Toronto and Hamilton, and made a report. I have had to deal with cases where there were only two employers who would not agree upon a man to represent them. If the employers all agree and say: We want one board of investigation and we will agree to have one man represent us on that board, a board will be granted at once. I have had cases of that kind in the smelter mines in western Canada. On one occasion four employers there agreed upon a man who should represent them on a board of conciliation and a board was appointed. There was, however, nothing of that kind here. The mayor of Thetford Mines, the President of this Western Federation of Miners and the secretary, whose letters my hon. friend has read, came to Ottawa at my request. The facts were these. These various corporations had increased the pay of their men by twenty-five cents a day the fall before and twenty-five cents a day again in April of last year, and in June they were willing to advance the men's pay by another twenty-five cents. Even with all these increases the wages would not be very high and, of course, wages were not so high then as they are now. Shortly before that we had had in that district two Boards of Conciliation which gave unanimous findings fixing the wages at 51.75 per day instead of $2.25, the representatives of the employers on those boards respectively agreeing with the representatives of the men, that 51.75 were the wages the men should get. I pointed that out to miners' representatives when they came to Ottawa: These companies will give you an advance of 25 cents a day more, and I think you

had better aceeipt it, because I am afraid if you have a commission to inquire into [DOT] the conditions, they will not give you as much as that; and I pointed out what those other two boards of conciliation had found, namely, that SI .75 were the correct wages. After their second visit, they left me thoroughly satisfied that they were going back with the intention of accepting the 25 cents advance, and that they would be satisfied with that.
Where were these two boards of conciliation the minister speaks of?

In Nova Scotia, and
the awards were unanimous. The men were doing somewhat similar work.
Mr, DEVLI'N:	Did the minister advise
the men of Thetford Mines that under the Act a board of conciliation could not be granted?
I think I did.
You did?
I think I did. I am not sure; I am speaking only from memory, but I think I would 'have done so.

That does not appear in
the correspondence.

I am sure, although
I do not just remember the matter of telling them, but that is the first thing that would strike me in a case where there were six employers. The six men must agree on a man to represent them or we cannot grant a board of conciliation. I sent Mr. Ar-cand the fair-wage officer whom we had at that time for the province of Quebec and the Maritime Provinces, and he did not succeed in reaching an adjustment or in inducing the parties to adjust the matters in dispute, and I took the course there that I have taken in many similar cases, that is, I appointed a commissioner, in the person of Mr. Blan-chet, a barrister of Ottawa, who speaks both English and French fluently. He -went down there and in a few days he got a perfectly satisfactory agreement signed up by two men from each of tne six mines, or twelve men in.all, some of them 'belonging to the Catholic Association and some belonging to the Western Federation of Miners. That agreement was perfectly satisfactory to everybody, and I was gratified at and fully satisfied with the work. Mr. Blanchet had done, and I am much surprised that my hon. friend, who is ia lawyer
and who very likely possesses a copy of the Industrial Disputes Act, did not advise these men to keep on working and tell them that Mr. Blanchet, a fair and just man, was being appointed as commissioner and that he would make an honest report, as he did.

Why did the minister
wait until a strike was declared?

I did not anticipate a strike; I supposed the men were going to carry out my advice. I paid their expenses to come to Ottawa 'because I thought I could talk the matter over with them better than I could discuss it by correspondence. This matter was brought up by two prominent Liberals from Montreal, more from a party standpoint than anything else, before the Trades and Labour Congress held in Toronto last fall, and the solicitor of that Congress, Mr. J. G. O'Donoghue, who has been their solicitor for a great many years and who is well known to many members of this House, when he learned of the facts, said: "The minister is quite right; he cannot grant a board of conciliation under the circumstances," and any legal gentleman reading over the statute would come to the same conclusion. At any rate, in the end we secured a settlement that was satisfactory to everybody.
Did the men get the increase of twenty-five cents a day?

Yes, and they went to work. I am very much afraid, to be frank with my hon. friend (Mr. Pacaud) that he did not make any effort to keep the thing iquiet. I was advised at the time that he and another prominent Liberal in the town of Thetford Mines addressed a public meeting of those men and inflamed them to going on strike.

I deny that absolutely. I am very much pleased that the minister has mentioned the matter. I understood that the Department of Labour had sent to Thetford Mines some Austrians from the com finement camps to work for the Asbestos Corporation. Immediately before I attended the meeting, which was the only one I addressed, I went and saw the manager of the mine and asked if the men had been sent at the request of that company, and I asked the department and they said they were short of labour. They had to get detectives to protect the Austrians and see them safely home at the end of their day's work, but even then one of them got killed.

I did attend the meeting, and I am proud of it.
Mt CROTHERS. Did you not denounce the Minister of Labour and the Government for not granting a Board?
I never mentioned a word about anything except the Austrians.
But you denounced the Minister of Labour and the Government in connection with that?
Yes.
And inflamed the crowd that was there?
I had a perfect right to attack the minister.

He had a perfect
right to attack the minister for sending the Austrians there.
I do not know what my hon, friend means about sending them there. These men went there quite properly.
If the minister sent them there, my hon. friend had a perfect right to attack him.

I did hot send them there in the first place, but if I had, the hon. member would not be right in denouncing me under the circumstances. Thousands of these Austrians are interned in different parts of the country. When the war broke out, the men interned were divided into two classes. The first class consisted of those who were suspected of being enemies; these men were interned, and have never been let out so far as I know. The other class consisted of men who had been dismissed from their positions because they were of Austrian or German birth. I am not finding fault with any one for that, but these men could not get work as they were of enemy birth, and many of them came to the Registrar and asked to be sent to the internment camp, where they could get something to eat and have their families taken care of, and this class were sent to the -internment camps in large numbers. Subsequently, when there was work to be done, the men of this second class were let out if they were not thought dangerous, and that has been done all over the country. I accept my hon. friend's denial, of course. He admits, however, that he was at the meeting and that he .denounced the Government. I submit that I did what was per-
fectly right in the circumstances, and under similar ercumstances I should do it again to-morrow. I have nothing to retract, and nothing to apologize for, and the solicitor of the Trades and Labour Congress approved of my action.
Who paid the expenses of these Austrians to go there?
The employer pays the fare in the first instance, but recoups himself out of the first money earned by the men. If they remain a reasonable length of time, however, their fares are refunded.
Did these Austrians come from the Abitibi district?
I think they came from the Spirit Lake district.
Surely the Government did not bring men 800 to 1,000 miles to work in the Thetford Mines?
I did not say the Government 'brought them, but the employer.
I know, but the original cost must have been paid by the Government.
You mean the cost of sending them there?"
And bringing them back?
No, the employer does that.
I know a good deal about those Austrians.

I am not a lawyer, and I am rather proud I am not in discussing a question like this, but the minister cannot claim ignorance of the law. He said a moment ago that the operators of these six mines should have got together.

I did not say they
should have; I said they might.

The minister blames
the men because they did not get the operators together.
No, I do not.
What was the reason for refusing a board? The minister said that the men would have to get a representative for each of the companies.
When I said that it would be necessary to have a representative for each of the operators, I meant that they would be given the opportunity of selecting them.
Very well. The minister says that at the outset they did not know how many mines there were in Thet-ford. That is a poor excuse.
That is what you say.

Do you mean to say that the Department of Labour or the Deputy Minister does not know how many mines there are in any mining camp in Canada? It is ridiculous to say that, and I am sure the deputy minister would not say it.

The number of mines is one thing, but the number of mines involved in the dispute is another, and we did not know the number of mines involved in this dispute.
Mr. VER'VILLE: It is all given in the letters that have been read.
I am speaking subject to correction, because I have not the correspondence here, but my recollection is that no intimation is given in the first letter of any company but one being involved.
I do not want to go over the whole correspondence again. It is all given in the application.
Does the application mention more than one employer?

I will not detain the House by reading it all, but I will give the names of the companies that are mentioned: Asbestos Corporation, Johnson Mines, Jacob Mining Company, Limited, Bell Asbestos Mines, Limited, Martin Bennett, Limited. That is more than one company, is it not? So the minister was wrong when he said the application concerned only one company.
In the letter they do not say anything about these different employers being in the dispute.

In the return I received there were three important letters missing, of the following dates, the 26th, 27th and 29th of June. These letters should have been in the return, but I suppose they were omitted through a mistake. I go't them elsewhere. I do not mean to say, that the minister is personally responsible for that, but the letters should have been in the return. As I have already said, the application was made on the 15th July, and the . minister wrote saying the men should have got together so that he could grant a board.
According to my understanding of the Lemieux Act, the minister is wrong. There have been cases before this, and I will cite one. The carpenters in Montreal some few years ago asked for a board, and although it was contrary to the law to grant one, a3 they were not a public utility, a majority of the men asked for a board and it was granted. In this case there was a builders' exchange.
It can only be done by consent of both parties. They all agreed upon one man in that case.
Surely the minister could have taken similar action in this case, instead of sending Mr. Blanchet down.
We sent Mr. Arcand, and he reported that they could not agree.
We are satisfied with the result.
Which result?
The one Mr. Blanchet got.

Two dollars a day! And this to support a family of five or six children, perhaps. Why, the minister could not buy cigars for that. It is a shame when any one says that men are satisfied with such conditions. Of course, I am not the sufferer, but how can anyone claim that he is satisfied because men are getting two dollars a day? The fact remains that these men have lost three weeks, or thereabouts. They were out on strike for that length of time-from the 3rd to the 23rd August. At $12 a week this would mean $36. Does the minister mean to say that these men will be able to make up that loss? It is his fault, and he knows it. I do not accept his statement that it would have been impossible to get these operators together and



to have a board appointed with a view to preventing a strike. It is true that the Trades and Labour Congress did favour the repeal of this Act. But I would be the first man to vote against that, and I have said so in the Congress.
Was the hon. member (Mr. Verville) in the Congress in 1911, when they voted in favour of the repeal of the Act?

I was always against the repeal of the Act, and am on record on that point in the Congress. I was man enough to tell them what I thought. The principle of the law is all right; it is the application of it that is bad. It has been poorly handled in many cases, and the hon. minister must know it. I suppose he will not express agreement with me in that. This strike ought to have been avoided, but what I wish to urge is more activity in these matters in the future. If there is the prospect of a strike anywhere the minister ought to use diligence and to appoint a board if netessary, so as to prevent the strike. The hon. minister says that this matter was brought up in Montreal by a Liberal. I am not a member of the Trades Council of Montreal, and so I cannot say whether the minister is correct in that or
10 p.m. not. But if he will tell me who was the man-
The hon. gentleman was at the congress.
But the minister said that it had been brought up in the Montreal Trades Council.
No, I said it had been brought up in the congress by a delegate from Montreal.
Who was he?
I am not going to tell you that. Look up the record of the congress.
The minister says that the man was a Liberal; does he know that to be the case?
Yes.

We have some men in the labour movement who are neither Liberals nor Conservatives, and if the man referred to is the one I think of, he is one of these-a Radical. I do not accept the .information given by the minister that in this case it was not possible under the law to appoint a board. Of course, I must
tMr. Terville.]
leave the discussion of that point to the lawyers, but at present I firmly believe that it was possible. But if there is impossibility in such cases, then it is time to change the law so as to make it more effective. I am only sorry that the men are satisfied with what they have received. I would not be satisfied with it-far from it. But I am discussing this matter with a view to the future, and I urge the minister to take steps in good time to prevent strikes.

I am not surprised that my hon. friend (Mr. Verville) is not satisfied. .Such men are never satisfied. They don't want'to be satisfied; they want to have a grievance. He expresses the hope that this discussion will cause me to be more active in trying to avoid strikes. It will not have the slightest effect upon me.
I did not suppose it would.
Can't teach you anything.

Ont moment, please.
I have been doing my level best for five years past to prevent strikes. When I hear i* of trouble brewing I send an officer to try I to prevent an outbreak of that trouble. And since I took charge of the department there have been fewer strikes in Canada in proportion to our population than in any other civilized country in the world. We hear a great deal about Australia where they have compulsory arbitration and all that sort of thing. Last year they had 330 strikes and lock-outs, and we had 75. They have a population of five millions and we have a population of eight millions. In the United States last year they had 3,330 strikes and lock-outs. Had they had no greater proportion than we had, they would have had only 800 or 900. While I have nothing to say against my predecessor, nor against the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), there have been fewer labour troubles in Canada within the last five years than there were ever before. I have done everything I could to prevent these troubles. In the case under discussion I thought the difficulty was settled when the men left Ottawa. So, my hon. friend from Maison-neuve need not waste time in expressing the hope that his efforts of to-night will help me in this matter. I have used diligence in these matters for the last five years, and I intend to follow the same course as long as I am in the department.
The hon. member says there were fewer strikes in Canada. I believe that. But where was there any room v for strikes?

There were more
strikes before the war than there have been since.
I Mr. MACDONALD:	The minister need
I not take credit to himself for that. The i simple reason is that the Canadian people \ were more patriotic than the people in j other countries, and were therefore anxious to avoid labour troubles during the : war. But the relatively small number of j labour troubles shows also the advantages j of the legislation which was introduced j hy my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. | Lemieux) by which compulsory investi-' gation is made possible with a view, to adjusting these matters.
I have always recognized that, and have ^always expressed myself in the strongest terms in favour of this Act. My hon. friend from Rouville knows that,

I represent a large labour constituency, (and one plea made against me in the last campaign was that I supported this Act, known as the Lemieux Act. In all the labour centres of this country the Conservative party, to the best of their ability, urged the view that this was a nefarious Act intended to cripple, the rights of labour and in a great many cases their candidates were pledged to repeal it. The minister is frank enough to say that he recognizes that this -is a good Act. I think that everyone will agree that the principle of the compulsory investigation of trouble previous to a strike is a sound one. But the minister'promised last year to give us some amendments of this Act and I am sorry that he has not introduced them. There is an imperfection in the Act which prevents the investigation of troubles that arise where an application is made by a body of organized labour on the one hand *nd employers who are made up of different companies on the other. If the Act does not permit compulsory investigation I would suggest to the minister that it would be wise on his part if he would at this session introduce a Bill by which the provisions of this Act might be made applicable to given situations of that kind. I have no doubt that in the labour difficulties that existed in the West, and which the minister was investigating during the
past winter, we had a situation where on the one hand we had a number of men belonging to one particular labour union and on the other hand numerous employers belonging to different companies. There ought not to be any technical difficulty existing by which provisions of this law should be prevented from being put into force in any labour district. If that is the difficulty that the minister speaks about, I would like to ask whether he considers it the part of wisdom to introduce- an amendment to deal with that and whether he will not do so.

The administration of the Act by my predecessor, Mr. King, and my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), disclosed to them certain difficulties which they would like to have overcome by amendments and the administration of the < Act has disclosed to me some more. I am ! finding no fault with the Act. Like every other Act which is new, you discover in its j administration and operation that it is capable of improvement. I anticipated what my hon. friend just suggested, three years ; ago, and I had a new Bill throughout prepared. I think it included about twenty alterations. Under the Act as it stands now you might have a difficulty arising between employer and employees as to the meaning of an award. In one case I had to appoint a second board to determine what the first board meant. One of the amendments I proposed was that a board might be reconvened for the purpose of reconsidering and determining what the award really did mean. I talked the matter over, the war came on, it was a controversial question, I was satisfied that we would be weeks and weeks discussing the matter, and I did not bring the Bill down because the war was on. I do not propose this ses- j sion to bring in any amendments. We are getting along pretty well; we would be bet- j ter with these amendments but I do not feel justified in bringing in a Bill of this j very controversial character at the present i time. I talked it over with the representative labour men and they did not agree as to what should be done. I do not think we would agree in this House as to what should be done and I therefore do not think it would be wise to introduce the Bill this year. -

The minister does
not need to introduce a whole Bill. It is an entirely technical matter. Manifestly the intention of the Act was that there
